answer_md:
Boeing's FY2025 filing presents meaningful commercial delivery recovery: BCA revenues increased by $18,633 million in 2025 compared with 2024, primarily due to higher deliveries across all programs, and net cash provided by operating activities was $1.1 billion in 2025, compared with net cash used of $12.1 billion during 2024, driven primarily by higher commercial airplane deliveries [1][2]. The 737 production rate recovered from below 38 aircraft per month at the beginning of the year to 42 per month during the fourth quarter, and the program plans to increase the production rate from 42 to 47 in 2026 with the concurrence of the FAA [3].

This recovery trajectory is directly conditioned on regulatory approval: since the 737-9 door plug accident in January 2024, the 737 program may only increase production rates and/or implement new production lines with the concurrence of the FAA, and there is risk that planned production rate increases may be delayed or not occur at all if Boeing's Safety Management System key performance indicators do not support them or if the FAA does not concur [4][5]. The 777X program deepens the tension: Boeing reassessed the anticipated timing to complete FAA certification flight testing in the third quarter of 2025, delayed first delivery of the 777-9 to 2027, and recorded an incremental reach-forward loss of $4,899 million during 2025, with the ultimate timing of certification to be determined by the regulators [6]. As of December 31, 2025, Boeing had approximately 35 737-7 and 737-10 aircraft in inventory while continuing to work through the certification process, illustrating how completed aircraft can remain undelivered while regulatory processes play out [3].

On supply chain, the filing simultaneously notes improving supply chain performance with fewer disruptions from production quality issues, global supply chain constraints and labor instability, while also warning that these factors continue to challenge overall productivity and adversely impact financial position, results of operations and cash flows [7]. New tariffs on goods imported from China, Canada, and Mexico, as well as new and modified tariffs on aluminum, steel, and copper imports implemented during 2025, could collectively have a material impact on Boeing's financial position, results of operations and/or cash flows, with Boeing's supply chain also being impacted by those tariffs and export restrictions [8]. China, described as a significant market for commercial aircraft, saw certain customers pause accepting deliveries in the second quarter of 2025 in response to ongoing tariff negotiations between the U.S. and China, creating a direct interruption to the delivery recovery narrative even though deliveries to those customers subsequently resumed [9].

Labor constraints add further pressure: IAM District 751 went out on strike for 53 days in 2024, halting production of most commercial aircraft, and IAM District 837 went out on strike for 101 days in 2025, disrupting St. Louis operations, while contracts with the Society of Professional Engineering Employees in Aerospace representing approximately 16,000 Boeing employees are scheduled to expire in October 2026 [10][11]. Despite the revenue improvement, BCA reported a loss from operations of $7,079 million in 2025, partly reflecting higher combined reach-forward losses of $5,283 million on the 777X and 767 programs, while aircraft order cancellations during 2025 totaled $11,094 million and net ASC 606 adjustments totaled $17,759 million, primarily relating to 777X and 787 aircraft [12][13].
